• Name: Red Claw Shrimp
  • Other names: Red Clawed Shrimp, Red Claw Prawn, Red Clawed Prawn, Chocolate shrimp, Red Rusty shrimp
  • Scientific names: Macrobrachium dayanum and Macrobrachium assamense
  • Type: Freshwater
  • Minimum tank size: 40 litres
  • Breeding: Medium-Difficult
  • KH: 4 – 16
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: Omnivore / Carnivore
  • Temperament: Aggressive
  • Life span: up to 3 years
  • Colour: translucent, blue, light straw, or brown with pink spots on the body

Red Claw Shrimp or Red Claw Prawn (Macrobrachium dayanum and Macrobrachium assamense) are among the rarest shrimp (prawn) species in the aquarium hobby, and very little is known about them. Unlike most Macrobrachium, which are a major source of food for humans, Red Claw Shrimp are suited to ornamental farming: they have a small size, high fecundity, low aggressiveness and interesting coloration.

The name 'Red Claw Shrimp' is technically not correct, as these crustaceans belong to the genus Macrobrachium and are therefore prawns. The name has nevertheless stuck.

Freshwater prawns of the genus Macrobrachium are decapod crustaceans of the family Palaemonidae. The genus is considered a descendant of a marine ancestor, and many species still depend on brackish water for breeding. Macrobrachium dayanum and Macrobrachium assamense are among the few species that have become completely acclimatised to freshwater and live in inland rivers and streams. The two species are extremely similar.

Macrobrachium assamense is divided into two subspecies: Macrobrachium assamense assamese and Macrobrachium assamense peninsular. Morphological data suggest it is in fact a single species. The differences are minor: M. a. assamese has a slightly longer rostrum (0.6–0.8 times the carapace length vs. 0.5–0.6 in M. a. peninsularis) and a more elongated carpus (3.5–4.0 times as long as broad vs. 3.0–3.5).

The biggest concern is their aggression, as they may attack other fish, snails, frogs, shrimp and even dwarf crayfish.

Red claw shrimp have a very limited distribution range.

Macrobrachium assamense is indigenous to North India (the Peninsular region) and is found in the Khoh river in the Garhwal region.

Macrobrachium dayanum occurs in southern India, the Bay of Bengal area, the Kaira River, and the Rajshahi area of Bangladesh.

They are bottom feeders, typically found in stagnant water or slow streams and rivers, under crevices of stones, logs, dead leaves and grassy vegetation.

In their natural habitat, they prefer areas with gravel, cobbles and bedrock with a little sand as the substrate.

The minimum recommended tank size for keeping Red claw shrimp (1 male and 1 female) is 40 litres.

A larger tank is always preferable for the stability of water chemistry, and it allows more diverse hiding areas to be set up. If you are going to breed them, consider having a separate tank for the offspring.

Temperature: the genus Macrobrachium is restricted to warmer areas. The ideal temperature for Macrobrachium dayanum and Macrobrachium assamense is 20 – 28°C. They do not like sudden temperature fluctuations. Shrimp taxonomist Werner Klotz noticed that they require at least subtropical water temperatures throughout the year; below about 15°C they largely stop being active and they die below 10°C.

pH: 7.0 to 8.5.

Hardness: they prefer hard water, with 6 – 20 GH and 4 – 16 KH.

It is never recommended to add shrimp to an uncycled tank: high ammonia and nitrates will kill them. A stable nitrogen cycle and stable water parameters are key.

Lighting: no special requirements. If you have plants, adapt the lighting to their needs. Although Red claw shrimp are nocturnal and do not really depend on light, their activity pattern is synchronised with the light/dark and feeding cycles.

Substrate: a rocky substrate breaks the line of sight. Red claw shrimp are less aggressive when they do not see the target, so this is safer for other tank mates as well.

Filtration: no special requirements, as long as the filter suits the size of the tank. Sponge filters or matten filters are recommended for small setups: they are cheap, easy to maintain and clean, provide a lot of surface to graze on and are great for hiding. Adult Red claw shrimp may sometimes chip and chew on the sponge filter.

Decorations (hiding places): decorations provide shelter and reduce stress, which is especially crucial for moulting, since cannibalism after moulting can become a big problem. There should be plenty of dark areas to hide. They appreciate all types of leaves, rocks, bricks, driftwood, PVC pipes, plastic mesh and other decorations. If you keep several, each needs hiding places in different parts of the tank, as they are territorial and do not like neighbours.

Plants: they will not completely destroy a planted tank as crayfish or crabs do, but they may eat, cut and shred some plants. Good options are plastic plants, floating plants, strong plants (such as Anubias and Java fern) and cheap plants you are ready to lose.

Acclimation: acclimate them very slowly to prevent unnecessary stress; 2 – 3 hours is generally good enough.

Like most Macrobrachium, Red claw shrimp are omnivores to carnivores and eat almost anything that comes their way. In the wild, gut analysis showed they consume detritus, diatoms, aquatic plants, algae, small invertebrates (worms, snails, aquatic insects) and small bottom-dwelling fish. Even sand was found in their stomachs.

Suggested foods in the aquarium:

  • blackworms
  • crushed snails
  • earthworms
  • brine shrimp
  • bloodworms
  • daphnia
  • detritus worms
  • dead fish or shrimp

They also accept frozen and commercial food as well as vegetables:

  • shrimp pellets
  • shrimp granules
  • fish food (TetraMin® flakes, etc.)
  • Hikari crustacean food such as Hikari Shrimp Cuisine
  • frozen bloodworms
  • blanched vegetables
  • dead plants
  • leaf litter

They are aggressive, greedy eaters and will try to take as much food as they can carry, even more than they can eat.

Feeding frequency: 3 – 4 times a week for adults; daily for juveniles.

Calcium and moulting: all crustaceans have a hard, multi-layered exoskeleton that does not grow with the animal, so shrimp must moult as they grow. Calcium is an essential component of the exoskeleton, so growing a new one requires a lot of it. Moulting leaves shrimp vulnerable. Before moulting, Red claw shrimp become less active, stop eating and seek shelter; otherwise they can easily fall prey to tankmates. It is crucial that they get enough calcium, which can be provided by regularly feeding specialised invertebrate foods or calcium-rich vegetables.

Red claw shrimp are aggressive and territorial. They are not social and do not like to be kept in dense groups. Males readily display aggression towards anything around them. There is a very high chance that they will attack small prey in the tank, such as dwarf shrimp, snails and even small fish, which makes them a really bad choice for a peaceful community tank. The genus Macrobrachium is territorial, aggressive and cannibalistic, and gets more dangerous as the animals grow.

They are nocturnal, becoming active almost exclusively at twilight and in darkness. In nature this is mainly associated with avoiding visual predators while feeding.

  • Social: No
  • Active: No
  • Peaceful: No
  • Burrowers: No

Tankmates: it can be risky to house multiple shrimp in the same tank; males in particular are extremely likely to fight and eventually kill one another. Ideally they are kept solitary, or in a group of one male with 1 – 2 females, which can reduce aggression. They will compete with tankmates for food, so make sure they are well fed.

Fish: they can coexist with fish, but there is always a risk of predation. Large and/or aggressive fish should be avoided, while small fish (such as neon tetras and guppies) and bottom-dwelling fish will disappear over time. Most fish are most vulnerable at night while resting near the substrate, which is exactly when Red claw shrimp are most active.

Dwarf shrimp and snails: best avoided, as Red claw shrimp will likely prey on them and eventually wipe them out. Even Amano shrimp may get caught.

Bad tankmates:

  • Larger or aggressive fish
  • Crayfish species
  • Freshwater crab species
  • Frogs

Both males and females reach maturity at about 5 months (male 5 cm in length; female 4 cm). Sexual dimorphism is prominent in adults.

  • Size: males are slightly larger and heavier than females. The cephalothorax and second walking legs are also larger and thicker in males.
  • Claws: mature males can be easily recognised by their longer and stronger chelipeds with larger spines than in females.
  • Genital pore: in males it lies between the bases of the fifth walking legs; in females it is at the base of the third walking legs, with a gap between them. Males have an appendix masculina on the second pleopods.
  • Pleopods: in females the first, second and third abdominal pleura are elongated and broad and form a brood chamber in which the eggs are carried between egg laying and hatching.
  • Ovaries: an egg-bearing female can easily be identified by the orange ovaries that occupy a large part of the cephalothorax.

Macrobrachium dayanum differs from Macrobrachium assamense by having a stouter carpus of the second cheliped in adult males.

Red claw shrimp have abbreviated larval development and can breed easily in freshwater aquaria. There are four distinct phases in the life cycle: egg, larva (zoea), post larva and adult. The time spent in each phase and the growth rate are affected by diet and environmental factors such as temperature.

Mating and spawning: during mating the male protects or guards the female with its large claws and shows aggression to other males. The female stays very calm near or under the male. Spawning takes place 18 – 22 hours after mating. At spawning the female bends forward to keep contact with the ventral thoracic region, forming a 'U'-shaped structure, and the eggs are extruded directly into the brood chamber through the genital pore.

Eggs: fertilised eggs are deep green, about 2.5 – 3.0 mm long and 1.52 – 2.0 mm wide. According to a study, fecundity ranges from 13 to 102 eggs in Macrobrachium assamense and from 43 to 195 in Macrobrachium dayanum, and is strongly correlated with the size of sexually mature females. Eggs in all stages of development are elliptical, with a diameter of 0.42 to 0.8 mm. Incubation lasts 14 to 24 days depending on temperature, for example around 14–18 days at 26–28°C. The eggs slowly change to yellow after a few days and develop black eyes in the final stage; their colour gradually becomes lighter and turns whitish grey when the larvae are fully grown.

Hatching: hatching takes about 1 – 2 hours. Eggs do not hatch below 25°C or above 30°C. Larvae are very active after hatching and live on the bottom straight away. They should be fed daily (ideally twice), without feeding so much that water quality deteriorates. Suitable foods:

  • newly hatched brine shrimp
  • artificial food for fish larvae (such as 50 or 100-micron golden pearls)

Currently there is no data on the maximum lifespan of Red claw shrimp in the wild. Under optimal conditions in a proper aquarium they can live up to 3 years.

Size: both species are 5 – 7.5 cm in total length and 3 to 7 g in weight. The carapace and abdomen are relatively translucent and can be banded with red and white lines. Depending on age and environment they can be blue, light straw or brown with pink spots on the body, and the tips of the walking legs are red. Juveniles are generally brown or creamy. Males become glossy and bluish-grey with red claws during the breeding season.
